dossier.summary: I am truly at a loss to explain how I managed to play this game all the way through more than once back in 2006. Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel – bastard child of the Fallout series. Hated by nearly everyone who loves the other Fallout games. I played it multiple times back in 2006, and when I learned that none of my predecessors at RPGFan had reviewed it, I knew it was my destiny to do so.
strengths: Brotherhood of Steel (BoS) is based in the Fallout universe that players of the series know so well, but it takes significant liberties with that universe.
One of the best things about the Fallout series has always been its meticulously detailed backstory, and for fans of the series, this is where BoS begins to go horribly awry.
This game is not considered canon, though, so the many details of how this game deviates from the rest of the Fallout games are best left to the already existing websites dedicated
This is an action RPG, so the plot doesn’t really get any deeper than that; but this is a Fallout game, even if in name only, and the bar for Fallout stories
It seems best to me to score it the way most players will approach it: as a Fallout game.
criticisms: Don’t be deceived, though – even if this were a review of Nukeytown: Sisterhood of Iron, it would still get a bad score.
Most frustrating is the fact that enemies with ranged attacks can see and attack at a much greater range than the player.
What really makes the game bad is the lack of any sort of interesting character variation or development.
The voice acting is much better than the music, but the dialogue is written badly enough that I generally chose to skip listening to it.
Boring to play, music doesn't match the game, poorly written.

Of course, this soon turns into a much larger mission that requires players to defeat a cult, kamikaze ghouls, and an army of Super Mutants.
Melee weapons and guns are both an option, and melee fighting does much more damage than ranged, which balances out the risk of getting up close and personal with enemies.
Unfortunately, BoS gets a number of things wrong that suck the fun out of combat, whether the player is a Fallout veteran or not.

What then takes place is a classic hackfest that's set in a post-apocalyptic world.

dossier.summary: Released in 2004 for PlayStation 2 and Xbox, Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel is a top-down action RPG that represents a significant departure from the series' roots. Unlike the tactical PC entries, it focuses on linear hack-and-slash combat. It is widely considered the "black sheep" of the franchise due to its non-canon status, nu-metal aesthetic, and controversial product placement. As of 2026, it remains one of the few entries not available on modern digital storefronts like Steam or GOG.
strengths: Players no longer navigated deep dialogue trees or complex moral choices; instead, they fought through waves of mutants and raiders in a style reminiscent of Gauntlet .
criticisms: In the TV show and games like Fallout: New Vegas , the Brotherhood is often criticized for its technological stagnation.
systems: Unlike the tactical PC entries, it focuses on linear hack-and-slash combat.
While the original games were complex, turn-based isometric RPGs, Brotherhood of Steel utilized the Snowblind Engine to deliver a real-time, linear experience.
Players no longer navigated deep dialogue trees or complex moral choices; instead, they fought through waves of mutants and raiders in a style reminiscent of Gauntlet .
Because it was built on the same technical foundation as Dark Alliance , it inherited that game's fluid combat and local co-op capabilities.
Fallout Tactics (2001) is a squad-based tactical combat game for the PC.

What Is the Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel 2004 Video Game?
In the early 2000s, the Fallout franchise was at a crossroads.
Interplay Entertainment, the original publisher, was facing severe financial difficulties.
Seeking to capitalize on the success of console action RPGs like Baldur’s Gate: Dark Alliance , the company decided to bring the post-nuclear wasteland to the PlayStation 2 and Xbox.
The result was Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel , released in January 2004.
This title was a significant advancement in terms of platform accessibility but a notable departure in gameplay mechanics.
